title: The CTCS(infinity) limit and the beta(2,1) coalescent
short_statement: Characterize the infinite critical beta-splitting CTCS limit and its exact relation to the beta$(2,1)$ coalescent.
open_problem: Give a complete probabilistic description of $\mathrm{CTCS}(\infty)$ and identify the exact mathematical relationship, if any, between its exchangeable partition dynamics and the beta$(2,1)$ coalescent.
background: Aldous's beta-splitting family is a fundamental model for random rooted binary trees, motivated in part by phylogenetic tree shapes. The critical beta-splitting case has splitting probabilities proportional to $1/(i(m-i))$ for a clade of size $m$, producing unusually balanced logarithmic phenomena and a rich connection between recursive tree structure, Markov chains, and exchangeable partitions. Aldous and Janson developed a continuous-time consistent splitting model $\mathrm{CTCS}(n)$ whose finite-$n$ trees are consistent under deletion of a uniform leaf. This consistency suggests an infinite exchangeable limit $\mathrm{CTCS}(\infty)$, analogous in spirit to continuum random tree limits but with different merger/splitting structure. Their later papers formalize exchangeable partition representations and fringe-tree limits. The remaining conceptual question is the exact relationship between this infinite critical splitting object and the beta$(2,1)$ coalescent.
full_statement: In the critical beta-splitting model, a clade of size $m$ splits into subclades of sizes $i$ and $m-i$ with probability proportional to $1/(i(m-i))$, independently down the tree. Aldous and Janson embed this discrete Markov-branching tree in a continuous-time consistent splitting model $\mathrm{CTCS}(n)$ with real edge lengths. The family $\{\mathrm{CTCS}(n):n\ge2\}$ is consistent under deleting a uniformly random leaf and pruning degree-two vertices, which leads to an infinite exchangeable limit $\mathrm{CTCS}(\infty)$ represented through nested exchangeable partitions. The open problem is to give a complete probabilistic description of this infinite object and its partition-valued dynamics. In particular, determine whether the genealogy or time-reversal of $\mathrm{CTCS}(\infty)$ is exactly the beta$(2,1)$ coalescent, a deterministic time change of that coalescent, a projection or size-biased transform of it, or merely shares some marginal split-size asymptotics.
known_results: Aldous and Janson constructed the consistent finite $\mathrm{CTCS}(n)$ family, proved detailed results for leaf heights and fringe distributions, and formulated an exchangeable infinite limit. Their Part III paper develops the exchangeable partition representation and fringe tree more explicitly, giving a concrete framework in which finite restrictions of $\mathrm{CTCS}(\infty)$ can be studied. Part IV gives sharper Mellin analysis of leaf heights and normal/large-deviation estimates. Kolesnik supplied contraction-method proofs for related height central limit theorems. These advances clarify many one-dimensional and fringe statistics, but they do not fully identify the partition dynamics with, or separate it from, the beta$(2,1)$ coalescent.

progress.summary: The exchangeable partition representation and fringe tree have been developed further in later papers, but the exact beta$(2,1)$ coalescent relationship remains unresolved.

counterexample_rationale: Finite-dimensional distributions of $\mathrm{CTCS}(n)$ can refute a proposed exact coalescent identity. A complete positive result needs exchangeable-partition process convergence.
alphaevolve_rationale: Symbolic and simulation search can compare finite merger rates and suggest time changes. The main work is probabilistic identification of an infinite exchangeable process.

literature.synthesis: The finite critical beta-splitting model is explicit, but its infinite limit is subtle because consistency is expressed through deletion and pruning rather than a simple forward growth rule. The CTCS construction gives a natural continuous-time object, and later exchangeable-partition work makes the limit more concrete. The beta$(2,1)$ coalescent appears as the plausible coalescent-side analogue, but equality of finite-dimensional transition rates, time changes, and projections must be pinned down. The open problem is a structural identification, not just another asymptotic estimate.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Compute finite-dimensional transition rates for partitions induced by $\mathrm{CTCS}(n)$ and compare them to beta$(2,1)$ coalescent rates. Look for exact time changes or size-biased projections.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A proposed coalescent identity must match all finite restrictions of the exchangeable partition process, not only the one-step split-size distribution or marginal leaf-height asymptotics. The verifier should check the time parameterization, deletion/pruning convention, and whether the claimed process is forward splitting, backward merging, or a size-biased projection. A negative result should identify a concrete finite-dimensional statistic, such as a two-step transition probability or joint law of nested restrictions, where $\mathrm{CTCS}(\infty)$ and the beta$(2,1)$ coalescent differ.
